lesson.title: No he terminado
lesson.subtitle: Keeping haber and its participle glued together: No he terminado, ¿Ya has comido?, Nunca he visto

hook.title: The Golden Rule of the Spanish Perfect Past: Never Split 'He + Participle'!
hook.content: In English, we constantly wedge words between 'have' and the participle: 'Have **you** eaten?', 'I have **not** finished', 'I have **never** seen', 'I have **already** spoken'. In Spanish, **he / has / ha / hemos / han + participle** is welded with titanium! Nothing — not *no*, not *nunca*, not *ya* ('already'), not even the subject *tú* or *usted* in a question — may ever step between them!

pattern.title: Where Do Negatives, Pronouns, and Subjects Go?
pattern.content:
• Negatives & object pronouns go in **FRONT** of haber: **No he terminado**, **No lo he visto**, **Nunca he comido aquí**.
• Subject pronouns in questions go either before haber or after the participle: **¿Has comido?** / **¿Ya has comido?**!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: I have never spoken with him

exercises.target_answer: no he terminado, no lo he visto, nunca he hablado con él, ¿has comido hoy?, lo hemos hecho
exercises.meaning: I have not finished, I have not seen it, I have never spoken with him, have you eaten today?, we have done it
exercises.explanation: haber + participle is an unbreakable two-word block.

exercises.prompt: Build 'I have not finished' by placing 'no' in front of the welded 'he + terminado' block:
Which of these is the ONLY grammatical way to say 'Have you seen my brother?'?
exercises.explanation: Never wedge tú between has and visto, and remember the personal 'a' before mi hermano!

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: I have never seen this city

summary.outcome: Produce negative and interrogative present-perfect sentences without splitting haber from its participle.

use_example.german: No he terminado hoy y no lo he visto.
use_example.english: I haven't finished today and I haven't seen it.

summary.takeaway: Think of he visto / he hablado / hemos hecho as a single compound word — nothing can step inside it.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next branch ([5081] De la mañana a la noche): chain daily reflexives from morning to night!

he.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre split into tener (possession: tengo un coche) and haber (auxiliary: he hablado, plus hay)!

has.etymology_derivation: Never separate haber from its participle!

hablado.etymology_derivation: Past participles after haber NEVER change for gender or number — always end in -o!

hecho.english_meaning: done, made (participle of hacer); fact (el hecho)
hecho.shift_rule: Double sound shift: factum → hecho (f→h AND ct→ch!)
hecho.etymology_derivation: Look at Latin factum → Spanish hecho: initial f- became silent h-, AND medial -ct- became -ch-!

visto.etymology_derivation: You already know it from 'Hasta la vista'!

terminar.context_translation: I want to finish the work.
terminar.etymology_derivation: English 'terminate' sounds like a robot; Spanish terminar is the everyday word for 'finish'!

no.etymology_derivation: Latin nōn → Spanish no. Negation in Spanish is beautifully direct: place no right before the verb cluster.

nunca.etymology_derivation: Can stand before the verb alone (Nunca voy) or after no + verb (No voy nunca).

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).
